results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**How long you must keep tax records**

The documents say you must keep records “as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.”  In practice that means you keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period‑of‑limitations (the time in which you can amend the return or the IRS can assess additional tax) runs out.  
The period of limitations for income‑tax returns is found in Table 3 of the publication and is the number of years after the return was filed (returns filed before the due date are treated as filed on the due date) [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)].

**Employment‑tax records**

If you have employees, you must keep all employment‑tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)].

**Asset records**

Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. Those records are needed to calculate depreciation, amortization, depletion, and basis for gain or loss. [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)]

**Other considerations**

Once records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do not discard them until you check whether they must be kept longer for other reasons (e.g., insurance or creditors) [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)].

So, in short: keep income‑tax records for the period of limitations, employment‑tax records for 4 years, asset records for the disposal‑period limitations, and review each record after it becomes non‑tax‑necessary to see if another entity requires it.

---



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
**1. Build a workplace safety program (OSHA)  
**• Define a safety‑and‑health program that “includes management leadership, worker participation, and a systematic approach to finding and fixing hazards.” and “regular workplace inspections are an important tool for identifying hazards and fixing them.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)  
**• Follow OSHA’s Recommended Practices for Safety and Health Programs.  The handbook lays out a step‑by‑step approach built around seven core elements: “Management leadership, Worker participation, Hazard identification and assessment, Hazard prevention and control, Education and training, Program evaluation and improvement, and Communication and coordination for host employers, contractors, and staffing agencies.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  
**• Under the Federal “General Duty Clause” you must provide “a place of employment which is free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm to employees.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  

**2. Identify, assess, and control hazards**  
- Conduct regular workplace inspections, and document any hazards found.  
- Pinpoint each hazard, determine its severity, and decide on control measures (e.g., engineering controls, administrative controls, or personal protective equipment).  
- Re‑evaluate hazards whenever work processes, equipment, or materials change. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6)  

**3. Train employees**  
- Provide job‑specific safety training so workers know how to perform tasks safely and recognize hazardous conditions.  
- OSHA offers a range of free resources, including “on‑site consultation” and “training resources” (e.g., OSHA Training Institute Education Centers and Outreach Training Program). [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=92)  

**4. Make your premises accessible to people with disabilities (ADA guidelines)**  

| Feature | What the ADA requires | Key specifications in the Small‑Business guide |
|---------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| **Entrance doors** | Doors must be at least 36 in. wide and use accessible hardware.  Handles that require a tight grasp are not allowed. | “Most entrances to stores and businesses use 36 inch
